chapters.title: Chapter 5: The Kalman Filter for Dynamic Hedge Ratios

lessons.title: The Kalman Filter Explained Without the Heavy Math

children.text: Lesson 17 showed the two bad options: freeze the hedge ratio and let it go stale, or periodically re-estimate it and accept sudden jumps. The Kalman filter offers a third option, updating the estimate a little every single day, using both what you already believed and what today's new data actually shows, without ever discarding the past or freezing in place.

body.text: The entire idea behind a Kalman filter fits in one sentence: new estimate equals old estimate, plus a weight between 0 and 1, times the surprise in today's new observation. That weight, computed automatically rather than chosen by guesswork, is what makes the update a genuine blend instead of either ignoring new data or overreacting to it.

children.text: An Everyday Version of the Same Idea

Picture a cricket fan tracking a batter's current form across an IPL season. After every innings, she updates her sense of how good the player is right now. She doesn't throw away everything she believed before and judge purely on today's score, one bad innings after months of good form barely moves her opinion. She also doesn't ignore a string of new scores just because her older impression was different, form genuinely changes over a season. What she actually does, without writing down any equations, is blend her prior belief with each new data point, weighting the new information by how convincing it is relative to what she already thought. That blending instinct is exactly what a Kalman filter formalizes.

Formally, there is a hidden "state", the thing being tracked, here a slowly time-varying level, and a noisy "observation", today's data point that gives an imperfect clue about that state. Every single day, the update takes the same shape.

body.caption: The new estimate is the old estimate, adjusted by the gain K_t times the "surprise": how far today's observation y_t sits from what the old estimate would have predicted.

children.text: Where the Weight (the "Kalman Gain") Comes From

markDefs.definition: How much the true state is believed to wander, or drift, on its own from one step to the next.
How noisy or unreliable a single new observation is believed to be.

children.text: The gain isn't picked by hand, it is computed automatically from two ingredients: the
, how much the true state is believed to wander on its own from one day to the next, and the

, how noisy a single day's data point is believed to be. A state that drifts a lot, or an estimate that is currently quite uncertain, pushes the gain higher, favoring the new observation. Noisy, unreliable observations push the gain lower, favoring the existing estimate.

body.caption: Q is the process variance (how much the state wanders per step), R is the observation variance (how noisy one data point is), and P is the filter's own running estimate of its uncertainty. Uncertainty grows by Q each step before the new observation shrinks it back down.

children.text: Worked Example: Four Days of Updates by Hand

Start with Lesson 6's static estimate, β ≈ 1.39, as the filter's seed, with Q = 0.1, R = 1.0, and an initial uncertainty P = 0.5. Four new, noisy daily observations arrive, gradually trending upward, consistent with the real drift Lesson 17 described.

body.text: Compare this to Lesson 17's staircase chart of monthly rolling re-estimates. That chart held a fixed value for a month, then jumped. This one moves a little every single day, always somewhere between where it already was and what the newest data suggests, never frozen and never lurching.

children.text: A Note on This Simplified Version

This lesson used the simplest possible case, tracking a level directly from noisy observations of that same level, to build the intuition without extra clutter. The real hedge-ratio application is slightly different: the observation is HDFC Bank's price, and it needs to be compared against a prediction that is ICICI Bank's price multiplied by the current β estimate, not compared directly. The update logic, old estimate plus gain times surprise, is identical. Lesson 19 extends this exact idea to that real case, coded fully in Python.

body.prompt: Continuing this lesson's worked example, Day 4 ended with P ≈ 0.284. A new observation arrives on Day 5. Using Q = 0.1 and R = 1.0, what is the Kalman gain K₅ for that day? (First find P at Day 5 before the update, then compute the gain.)

body.title: What pushes the gain higher?
body.question: Which situation would push the Kalman gain toward a HIGHER value, meaning the filter trusts new observations more relative to its existing estimate?
options: A low process variance (Q) and a high observation variance (R)
A high process variance (Q) and a low observation variance (R)
Q and R do not affect the gain at all
The gain is always fixed at 0.5
body.explanation: A high process variance means the true state is believed to change a lot on its own, so recent data matters more. A low observation variance means each new data point is trustworthy. Both push the gain higher, toward trusting new observations. The opposite combination, low Q and high R, pushes the gain lower, toward trusting the existing estimate.

cards.definition: The hidden quantity being tracked over time, such as a slowly time-varying hedge ratio, that cannot be observed directly, only estimated.
A single new, noisy data point that gives an imperfect clue about the current state.
How much the true state is believed to wander, or drift, on its own from one step to the next.
How noisy or unreliable a single new observation is believed to be.
A number between 0 and 1, computed automatically each step, that determines how much weight the new observation gets relative to the existing estimate.

points: The Kalman filter's core update rule is: new estimate = old estimate + gain × (new observation − old estimate). It is a weighted blend, updated fresh every step, not a discrete reset or a frozen number.
The gain is computed automatically from the process variance (how much the true state drifts on its own) and the observation variance (how noisy each new data point is), not chosen by hand.

In this lesson's hand-worked example, starting from β ≈ 1.39 and four rising observations, the filter's estimate moved smoothly to about 1.509 over four days, gradually tracking the drift rather than jumping to it.

This lesson used a simplified version, tracking a level directly, to build intuition. The real hedge-ratio application compares an observed price against a prediction scaled by the other stock's price, using the identical update logic.
Lesson 19 codes this exact update rule in Python and applies it to a real pairs-trading hedge ratio.
